title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that tested whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) producing model_calls_used = 200 (preregistered maximum_model_calls for independent per‑arm generation = 400). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure, and give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial injection budgeting, and exploratory reserve usage) for informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived (execution/*, analysis/*).

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises productivity gains for network operations (NetOps), but it also creates operational safety risks: an incorrect or ill‑timed change may break reachability, violate access controls, or cause outages. The NetOps research community therefore advocates tooling that grounds LLM outputs—deterministic validators, sandboxed replay, and generate–validate–repair loops—to reduce hallucination‑driven or constraint‑violating changes.

Prior prototype and survey work documents these architectures and reports domain‑dependent improvements when LLMs are augmented with deterministic tooling; however, effect sizes depend critically on evaluation semantics, generation budgets, and the fidelity of verifiers and simulators. To provide an example of a reproducible, workflow‑centred confirmatory test, we preregistered and executed a paired experiment (study_id = cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) that directly compared an LLM baseline to a guarded verifier pipeline on synthetic NetOps intent→configuration tasks.

Research question. How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic validator → optional repair) change the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe network‑change proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts?

Contributions. (1) A complete, preregistered paired experiment with deterministic artifacts for N=200 tasks, including raw LLM outputs, scoring JSONs, and analysis traces; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the confirmatory hypothesis was non‑informative in this execution (shared generation semantics + zero baseline unsafe rate + budgeting choices); (3) concrete, archive‑supported design recommendations for informative repeats (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial injection to target baseline unsafe rates ≈10–15%, and exploratory ROC estimation). We make no efficacy claims about verifier superiority—the executed run did not produce evidence for or against such an effect because the confirmatory estimand was untestable under the chosen execution semantics.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and prototypes document rapid interest in LLMs for NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, automated remediation), and several works propose augmenting LLMs with deterministic tools, validators, or retrieval/simulator pipelines to improve correctness [https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12729; https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7132138; https://doi.org/10.1109/ojcoms.2026.3680457]. Methodological proposals such as generate–validate–repair and divide–verify–refine show reductions in constraint violations on curated benchmarks, but those gains are sensitive to verifier fidelity and generation semantics [https://openalex.org/W4412888330; https://openalex.org/W7161354925]. Guardrail and red‑team literatures emphasise trade‑offs (false refusals vs unblocked unsafe proposals) and call for workflow‑centred, replayable evaluations using deterministic sandboxing and archived scoring traces [https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.177004277.71795055/v1; https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.177006109.97957916/v1].

Our paper contributes a reproducible, preregistered instance of such an evaluation and highlights an executional failure mode—lack of per‑arm variability due to shared generation semantics—that can render a paired causal contrast untestable even when all other elements are deterministic and archived.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered as cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1. The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (SAFE encoded as 1). The confirmatory design was a paired binary comparison with N=200 unique tasks paired across two pipelines. The primary test was an exact McNemar two‑sided test implemented by paired_binary_analysis_v1 and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10000 resamples and seed = 1729. These analysis parameters are archived in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl.

Task generation and sampling plan. A deterministic generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks under a preregistered RNG schedule (seed = 42 and per‑task seeds 1..200). Tasks target operationally meaningful changes limited to admin/mtu/vlan fields across single‑AS multi‑device topologies; each task includes an explicit required_sequence and initial/final states (see execution/task_manifest.jsonl). The preregistration specified two task clusters (benign, adversarial) where adversarial prompts apply templated obfuscations and negation transforms intended to increase baseline unsafe rates.

Pipelines, validators, and scoring. Two pipelines were compared: baseline (LLM‑only candidate) and guarded (LLM candidate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional single repair). deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed deterministic sandboxed validation and produced per‑episode scoring JSONs that include normalized_configuration, parsed command counts, validator verdicts (valid: true/false), violation lists, and validation_before/after traces. In the confirmatory episodes no automatic repairs were applied (repair_provider_trace = null); binary outcomes (SAFE vs UNSAFE) derive directly from the validator's final verdict recorded in execution/scoring/*.json.

Generation semantics and model budget. The preregistration allowed two generation semantics: independent per‑arm generation (two LLM calls per pair) or shared_initial_candidate (one LLM call per pair shared across arms). Independent per‑arm generation is required to induce natural per‑arm variability when measuring the causal effect of a validator on outputs. The executed run used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json. That choice reduced model_calls_used to 200 (one call per task) relative to the preregistered maximum_model_calls=400 allocated for independent generation. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json).

Confirmatory analysis and missingness rules. The primary analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 producing a 2×2 contingency table (n11, n10, n01, n00), exact McNemar p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Preregistered missingness rules allowed one retry for failed model calls, replacement for contaminated tasks, and abort/downgrade if technical failures exceeded 10% of pairs. Execution produced no technical failures or exclusions; missingness_summary artifacts confirm complete_pair_count = 200.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The executor completed planned_episode_count = 400 (200 paired tasks × 2 pipeline scorings derived from a single shared initial generation per task) with failed_episode_count = 0. Model accounting recorded model_calls_used = 200 (execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/model_configuration.json). Deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false for the shared_initial_generation stage.

Primary confirmatory outputs. Analysis artifacts (analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) report baseline SAFE = 200/200 and guarded SAFE = 200/200, producing a paired contingency of n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). These values are preserved verbatim in analysis/results.json and the CSV artifacts.

Representative diagnostics. Scoring JSON examples (execution/scoring/task-000001‑baseline.json and task-000001‑guarded.json, similarly for task-000002 and task-000003) show identical shared_initial_candidate content across arms and validator traces reporting violation_count = 0 and valid = true in both validation_before and validation_after blocks. No repair_provider_trace entries are present for confirmatory episodes, confirming no automatic repairs altered the shared candidate. The combined facts below explain the non‑informative outcome.

Artifact‑grounded testability diagnosis. Three archive‑verifiable facts caused a ceiling/testability failure for the preregistered estimand:
1) shared_initial_candidate generation semantics were executed (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical LLM candidates for baseline and guarded arms (execution/model_configuration.json; execution/responses/*.txt). 2) the baseline observed unsafe‑proposal rate was 0.0 for the declared model and sampled tasks (baseline SAFE = 200/200; analysis/condition_summary.csv). 3) budgeting choices reduced model_calls_used to 200 vs preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400, limiting per‑arm variability. When a shared candidate is SAFE under the validator and no repairs are applied, both arms necessarily record SAFE; concordant pairs (n11) preclude discordant outcomes required by McNemar inference, collapsing the CI and yielding p = 1.0.

Exploratory reserves and sensitivity. The preregistration reserved up to 50 exploratory tasks to estimate verifier ROC and refusal tradeoffs; that reserve was not consumed for confirmatory testing. No technical failures occurred; therefore preregistered sensitivity analyses treating failures as safe or unsafe were not invoked. All artifacts referenced above (execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, analysis/*) permit deterministic replay and exact replication of the accounting described.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and scientific scope. The executed run does not provide evidence that deterministic validators are unnecessary nor evidence of verifier efficacy: it demonstrates a methodological failure mode where a well‑specified paired design becomes untestable when per‑pair generation semantics eliminate per‑arm variability and baseline unsafe rates are zero. The scientific contribution is therefore methodological and reproducible: we show how specific execution semantics (shared generation + constrained model budget) interact with power assumptions to create a ceiling effect. The complete deterministic artifact bundle allows independent verification of each numeric statement above.

Recommendations for informative repeats (artifact‑grounded). These recommendations follow directly from the preregistration and execution artifacts and are implementable without inventing new tooling:
(1) Use independent per‑arm generation for paired causal contrasts. For N=200 tasks, independent generation requires roughly 200 additional LLM calls (preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 vs executed 200). The manifest entries document exact model_call accounting and should be included in any repeat's preregistration. (2) Calibrate adversarial injection so baseline unsafe rate ≈10–15% to match the power plan. The power_and_precision_plan in the preregistration assumed baseline ≈10–15% and target paired reduction ≈7 percentage points; achieving that operating point requires stronger adversarial transforms or an explicit adversarial injection fraction. (3) Use the exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) to estimate verifier ROC and refusal tradeoffs before confirmatory testing; archive ROC estimates and CIs. (4) Make model_call accounting explicit in the preregistration and report executed vs planned calls in the manifest; budget trade‑offs should be justified quantitatively. (5) If budget forces a choice, prioritise independent per‑arm draws over wider model panels for paired causal tests because paired contrasts require per‑arm variability.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: execution semantics (shared vs independent generation) are an internal design choice that directly affected identifiability of the estimand; we documented the choice and its consequences in execution/model_configuration.json and deterministic_reconciliation.json. Construct validity: SAFE/UNSAFE labels derive from deterministic_netops_validator_v5's full_intent_constraint_validation; validator completeness relative to real production failure modes is unproven, and the verifier may under‑ or over‑approximate operational risk. External validity: tasks are synthetic single‑AS topologies generated deterministically; results do not generalise to multi‑AS, vendor‑specific, or production telemetry conditions. Conclusion validity: because the baseline unsafe rate was zero, the test had no discordant pairs and therefore no statistical power to detect a verifier effect; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline and independent generation (see preregistration's power_and_precision_plan).

Operational implications. Practitioners evaluating verifier augmentation must ensure that evaluation semantics permit per‑arm variability (independent generation) or use alternative estimands (e.g., absolute unsafe rate under single‑arm interventions) when model budgets are constrained. Moreover, pre‑confirmatory ROC estimation using an exploratory reserve reduces the risk of uninformative confirmatory runs. The artifact bundle includes concrete examples (execution/scoring/task‑00000X‑*.json) that illustrate how validator traces can be used to adjudicate correctness and to design adversarial injections tailored to a specific model's failure modes.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing an LLM baseline and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. The contribution is methodological and reproducible: (1) we publish a complete preregistered run with deterministic artifacts that permit exact replay; (2) we provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) we provide concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial budgeting, exploratory ROC estimation) to design informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the supplied bundle (execution/*, analysis/*) to support deterministic replays and community replication.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
